items.followUp: Differentiate between a saturated solution and an unsaturated solution.

rubric.why: An unsaturated solution has not reached its solubility limit.
rubric.description: States that an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at the given temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing its capacity to dissolve additional solute.

rubric.why: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution normally holds at that temperature.
rubric.description: States that a supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct comparison with a saturated solution.

modelAnswer: An unsaturated solution contains less solute than it can dissolve at a given temperature, so it can dissolve more solute.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution can normally hold at the same temperature; it is unstable and excess solute may crystallize out.

items.followUp: Calculate the concentration (% v/v) when 12 cm³ of ethanol is present in 80 cm³ of solution.

rubric.why: The percentage by volume is calculated using the volume of solute divided by the total volume of solution, multiplied by 100.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula or equivalent substitution.

rubric.why: The stated volumes give a concentration of approximately 5.56% v/v.
rubric.description: Calculates and states the concentration with the correct unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 5.56% v/v or a suitably rounded equivalent.

modelAnswer: Given: volume of acetone = 5 cm³ = 5 × 10⁻⁶ m³; volume of solution = 90 cm³ = 9 × 10⁻⁵ m³.
Formula: % v/v = (volume of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100.
Substitution: % v/v = (5 × 10⁻⁶ m³ ÷ 9 × 10⁻⁵ m³) × 100.
Answer: concentration = 5.56% v/v.

items.followUp: Describe how to prepare 500 cm³ of a 1 M NaOH solution.

rubric.why: One dm³ of a 1 M solution contains one mole of NaOH, whose molar mass is 40 g mol⁻¹.
rubric.description: Calculates the required mass of NaOH as 40 g.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct mass, with or without showing the molar-mass calculation.

rubric.why: The solution must be made up to a final volume of 1 dm³, rather than adding 40 g to 1 dm³ of water.
rubric.description: Describes dissolving the NaOH and making the solution up to 1 dm³ with distilled water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct preparation procedure and final volume.

modelAnswer: For 1 dm³ of a 1 M solution, required NaOH = 1 mol.
Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol⁻¹.
Mass of NaOH required = 1 mol × 40 g mol⁻¹ = 40 g.
Weigh 40 g of NaOH and dissolve it in a small amount of distilled water.
Transfer the solution to a 1 dm³ volumetric flask, add distilled water up to the mark, and mix well.

items.followUp: What is an alloy? Give one example of an alloy and name its components.

rubric.why: An alloy is a mixture, not a chemical compound, and is described as homogeneous.
rubric.description: Identifies an alloy as a homogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description of the mixture.

rubric.why: An alloy contains two or more metals, or a metal combined with a non-metal.
rubric.description: States the types of elements that form an alloy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the possible components.

modelAnswer: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal.

items.followUp: Why is gold less reactive than sodium?

rubric.why: Silver and gold have little tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
rubric.description: Explains their low reactivity by their low tendency to lose electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this chemical explanation.

rubric.why: Silver and gold are low in the metal reactivity series.
rubric.description: Places silver and gold near the bottom of the reactivity series.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly relating their low reactivity to their position in the series.

modelAnswer: Silver and gold have a very low tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
They are placed near the bottom of the reactivity series, so they are among the least reactive metals.

items.followUp: Write two chemical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Metals commonly react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic.
rubric.description: Gives one correct chemical property of metals, such as reaction with oxygen to form oxides.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct property, with a suitable example or equation.

rubric.why: Many metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen, or react with water to form a hydroxide or oxide and hydrogen.
rubric.description: Gives a second correct chemical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a distinct correct property, with a suitable example or equation.

modelAnswer: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic; for example, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
Many metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen; for example, Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.

items.followUp: What are halogens? State the colours of bromine and iodine.

rubric.why: Halogens are the non-metallic elements of Group VIIA (Group 17), known as salt-formers.
rubric.description: Defines halogens by their group or salt-forming nature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as Group VIIA/17 elements or as salt-forming non-metals.

rubric.why: Halogens have characteristic colours; chlorine is greenish-yellow and bromine is reddish-brown.
rubric.description: Gives correct colours for two halogens.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correct halogen colours.

modelAnswer: Halogens are the non-metallic, salt-forming elements of Group VIIA (Group 17) of the periodic table.
Chlorine is greenish-yellow and bromine is reddish-brown.

items.followUp: Define isotopes and describe the isotopes of chlorine using their proton and neutron numbers.

rubric.why: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between atomic number, mass number, and neutrons.

rubric.why: Protium has one proton and no neutrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct proton and neutron numbers, or equivalent isotope notation.

rubric.why: Deuterium has one proton and one neutron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct proton and neutron numbers, or equivalent isotope notation.

rubric.why: Tritium has one proton and two neutrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct proton and neutron numbers, or equivalent isotope notation.

rubric.why: Each hydrogen isotope has one electron in the first (K) shell; the shell diagrams should show this electron around the nucleus.
rubric.description: Shows the electron arrangement for the hydrogen isotopes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing or stating one electron in the K shell for the isotope diagrams.

modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number but different mass numbers because they contain different numbers of neutrons.
Protium: ¹₁H; nucleus = 1 proton, 0 neutrons; diagram: K shell with 1 electron.
Deuterium: ²₁H; nucleus = 1 proton, 1 neutron; diagram: K shell with 1 electron.
Tritium: ³₁H; nucleus = 1 proton, 2 neutrons; diagram: K shell with 1 electron.
In each diagram, draw a nucleus containing the stated protons and neutrons, then draw one electron on the first (K) shell around it.
